items.topic: Asymmetric P&L and Seasonal VAR Limitations
items.definition: The observation that many energy assets have lopsided, seasonally-driven P&L profiles that a single VAR number struggles to capture.
items.core_idea: Assets like peaking power plants sit idle and lose small amounts most of the year, then earn large windfall profits on a handful of hot summer afternoons; a gas pipeline selling firm delivery does the opposite, earning steadily until a rare failure causes a large loss. Season-specific VAR distributions could help but aren't a general fix, since not every asset's risk follows a clean seasonal pattern.
key_points: Energy P&L is often not normally distributed — gains and losses aren't equally likely.
A peaking plant loses small, steady amounts most days and earns rare large windfalls on hot summer afternoons.
A firm-delivery gas pipeline earns steady profits until an equipment failure causes a large loss; failures have some seasonality but far less than temperature-driven power demand.
Season-specific VAR distributions are a possible partial fix but not a general solution across asset types.
VAR remains useful precisely because it is simple and gets checked regularly, even though no general model can handle every special case.
relationships: Illustrates limits of one-sided/two-sided VAR framing
trading_implications: Risk limits sized off a single VAR number may understate the true tail risk of assets with option-like, seasonally concentrated payoffs (e.g., peaking plants).
common_misunderstandings: That a single VAR distribution fairly represents assets whose risk is concentrated in rare seasonal events rather than spread evenly through the year.

items.definition: The magnitude of money that could be lost if a counterparty defaults on a contract.
items.core_idea: The simplest way to estimate credit exposure assumes total loss on every contract, which bounds the worst case but overstates the likely loss; a more accurate estimate factors in the probability of recovering assets through bankruptcy, including where a given debt ranks in the recovery order (e.g., preferred debt is repaid before other debt).
key_points: Assuming complete loss on every contract sets an upper bound but tends to overestimate actual severity.
A more accurate estimate incorporates expected recovery through bankruptcy proceedings.
Recovery depends on debt priority — preferred debt is repaid ahead of other claims, so knowing where a contract ranks matters.
relationships: One of two components of counterparty credit risk, alongside credit quality
trading_implications: Firms set hard exposure limits per counterparty; overestimating exposure needlessly restricts trading, while underestimating it risks a catastrophic loss on default.

items.definition: A forward-looking assessment of how likely a counterparty is to default on its payment obligations.
items.core_idea: Credit quality draws on external ratings agencies plus in-house research on key counterparties, and can require multiple layers of analysis since a counterparty's own credit risk depends partly on the credit quality of its clients; a firm also becomes more likely to default once its large trades have moved against it, and less likely once trades have moved in its favor.
key_points: Forward-looking, relevant because many energy contracts run for years.
Ratings agencies provide a baseline; firms often supplement this with in-house research on important counterparties.
Assessment can require layered analysis — a counterparty's credit risk depends on the credit quality of its own clients.
A counterparty's default likelihood shifts with how its large trades have performed: less likely to default if trades favor it, more likely if trades have moved against it.
relationships: One of two components of counterparty credit risk, alongside credit exposure
trading_implications: Monitoring how a major counterparty's other large positions are performing can be an early warning signal for rising default risk, independent of published credit ratings.

items.definition: The practice of balancing credit risk controls against the need to keep doing business.
items.core_idea: Credit risk from bilateral energy agreements can't be eliminated outright, only mitigated with collateral and managed through supervision; controls that are too strict block legitimate trading and damage relationships, while controls that are too loose risk a catastrophic counterparty collapse, so firms need to find a middle ground.
key_points: Credit risk can be mitigated (collateral) and managed (supervision), but not eliminated.
Overly strict exposure limits cost missed trading opportunities and damaged relationships.
Overly loose limits risk a catastrophic loss from a counterparty collapse.
The goal is a balance between these two extremes, not a maximal-safety posture.
relationships: Builds on Credit Exposure and Credit Quality
trading_implications: Setting per-counterparty exposure limits is inherently a trade-off exercise, not a pure risk-minimization problem.
common_misunderstandings: That tighter credit controls are always safer — excessively strict limits carry their own business cost by blocking otherwise-good trades.

items.definition: The risk that the methodology or assumptions behind a valuation model become invalid over time.
items.core_idea: Energy model risk is especially acute because many models value long-lived physical assets (power plants, pipelines, gas wells with 20+ year lifetimes) using assumptions that regulatory change, population shifts, or technology can invalidate years later, compounded by employee turnover leaving no one who fully understands an aging model.
key_points: Poor assumptions and badly designed models cause risk problems across financial markets generally, but are especially common in energy given model complexity and long asset lifetimes.
A model can be adequate when built and still fail well before the asset's life ends, as regulations, population, or technology shift underlying assumptions.
Employee turnover compounds the problem — original model developers are often gone before issues surface.
Organizations need a deliberate process to ensure someone still understands each model in production after years of use.
relationships: Distinct risk category alongside VAR and counterparty/credit risk
trading_implications: Long-lived asset valuations (power plants, pipelines, wells) should be periodically re-validated rather than trusted indefinitely once built.
common_misunderstandings: That a model validated at inception remains reliable for the full life of a long-dated asset.

items.topic: Basis Risk at Illiquid Trading Points
items.definition: A model-risk source arising from approximating an illiquid physical trading point's price using a nearby liquid hub's price.
items.core_idea: Since many physical delivery points aren't liquid enough to price directly, models commonly assume the point moves in tandem with a nearby hub; this assumption holds up well sometimes, but the historical relationship between the two locations can break down over a period of years.
key_points: Illiquid physical points are commonly approximated using a nearby hub's price.
The implicit assumption is that the illiquid point tracks the hub's price changes.
This relationship can hold for a while and then break down after a couple of years, invalidating models built on it.
relationships: A specific instance of Model Risk
trading_implications: Basis relationships used to price or hedge illiquid delivery points should be periodically re-checked rather than assumed permanent.

items.definition: A model-risk source specific to spread options, where valuation is highly sensitive to the assumed correlation between the two underlying assets.
items.core_idea: Unlike some inputs, the correlation between two assets underlying a spread option can't be pulled from an independent market source — it must be estimated internally and reviewed regularly, making it a persistent source of valuation uncertainty.
key_points: Spread option value is highly sensitive to the correlation assumption between the two underlying assets.
Correlation can't be readily observed from an independent market source, unlike a traded price.
Because it must be estimated, correlation assumptions require ongoing review rather than a one-time calibration.
relationships: A specific instance of Model Risk
trading_implications: Spread option books carry embedded model risk that doesn't show up as clearly as price risk, since the key correlation input isn't independently observable.

items.definition: A trading position taken to lock in the profit or loss of another investment, transferring risk from one trader to another.
items.core_idea: The contract used to hedge is called the hedging instrument, and the position being protected is the hedged item; traders hedge particularly when liquidating the original position would be undesirable, difficult, or impossible — for example, a wind farm's bondholders may require hedges to lock in future income and guarantee bond payments, at the cost of forgoing upside if prices later rise.
key_points: Hedge = the trading position taken to offset risk; hedging instrument = the contract used; hedged item = the original position being protected.
Hedging transfers risk between traders rather than eliminating it.
Useful when the original position can't easily be liquidated or sold.
Example: bondholders financing a wind farm may require hedging (e.g., selling power forward) to guarantee the project can meet bond payments — but this locks out any upside from a future price rise.
relationships: Distinct risk-transfer concept from VAR, credit risk, and model risk
trading_implications: Hedging requirements imposed by lenders (e.g., project finance bondholders) can force a producer to give up upside price exposure in exchange for guaranteed cash flow.

items.topic: The Cost and Risk-Management Blind Spot of Hedging
items.definition: The idea that hedging is never free and can itself introduce underappreciated risk-management problems.
items.core_idea: Hedging carries a hidden cost because there are only a limited number of counterparties willing to take the other side — most commodities are ultimately bought by consumers who won't lock in prices more than a year or two out. Separately, because a hedge is booked as a distinct position, it often receives far less scrutiny than the original investment, even though it's equal in size and opposite in direction — creating a risk that an large position gets offset by an equally large opposing trade under the banner of "risk management" without the same level of review.
key_points: Hedging has a real, often hidden cost since willing counterparties for long-dated fixed prices are scarce — most consumers won't lock in prices beyond a year or two.
Producers want fixed prices to make projects financeable with outside capital (e.g., bondholders), but the limited counterparty pool constrains this.
A hedge is equal in size and opposite in risk to the original investment, yet typically gets much less scrutiny.
This scrutiny gap can let a large position be effectively reversed under the guise of hedging, undoing the original investment thesis without the same review it originally received.
trading_implications: Hedges should be reviewed with the same rigor as the position they offset, since a hedge desk can otherwise take on a large opposing bet with less oversight than the original trade.
common_misunderstandings: That hedging is a costless or purely risk-reducing action — it has real transaction/availability costs and can introduce its own governance risk.

items.definition: Accounting rules that let a hedger avoid mark-to-market treatment of the hedged item, provided the hedge and hedged item pass certain qualifying tests.
items.core_idea: Hedging often pairs a tradable instrument (like a futures contract) with a nontradable one (like a power plant's future output), and the two aren't naturally valued the same way; hedge accounting rules exist to address this mismatch by letting the hedged item skip mark-to-market treatment when specific tests are met.
key_points: Arises because hedges often combine tradable investments with nontradable ones, valued differently by default.
Hedge accounting lets the hedger avoid mark-to-market accounting for the hedged item specifically — not automatically, only if qualifying tests are passed.
relationships: Relates to Mark-to-Market Accounting and Historical Cost Accounting
trading_implications: Whether a hedge qualifies for hedge accounting treatment affects how much P&L volatility shows up on the books, even when the underlying economics are unchanged.
common_misunderstandings: That any hedge automatically qualifies for favorable accounting treatment — it depends on passing specific tests.
